name: Wood Buffalo National Park
blurb: Wood bison, wolves and whooping cranes on a vast northern delta.

tip.title: Remove the wood bison
tip.text: Wolves here rely on wood bison. Set Wood bison to -100% and watch the wolf, then the moose, beavers and cranes it must turn to.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Wood Buffalo National Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Long summer days power the sedge meadows, willows and forest of the far north.
Fire renews boreal forest and open meadow, resetting plant growth across the landscape.
Sedges form some of the large grass and sedge meadows UNESCO highlights in the park; they feed wood bison.
A willow of wet ground. Wood bison eat willow leaves in summer, and beavers and moose browse willows.
A main conifer of the boreal forest, whose seeds feed red squirrels.

nodes.name: Dwarf red blackberry
nodes.desc: A low forest-floor berry plant recorded near the park; its fruit is eaten by bears and foxes.

nodes.name: Wood bison
nodes.desc: The park holds the world's largest wood bison herd. They graze grasses, sedges and forbs, and dig through snow for food.
A large browser of willows and other woody plants, and a main prey of wolves and bears.

nodes.name: North American beaver
nodes.desc: Eats willow and sedges and builds dams; satellite images in 2007 revealed a dam about 850 m long in the park.
A small grass-eating rodent of meadows, eaten by foxes, bears and many other predators.
A forest squirrel that eats conifer seeds; lynx, foxes and wolves are recorded eating it.
A dabbling duck of the delta wetlands that eats plant matter and small aquatic animals.
A scavenger and egg thief, recorded more than any other bird in the park area.
Hunts voles, squirrels, ducks and eats berries; it is also a predator of crane nests.
A forest cat that preys on red squirrels and beavers according to GloBI records.

nodes.name: American black bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore eating berries, grasses, voles and moose, and a recorded predator of crane nests.
UNESCO says the park is the only place where the wolf and wood bison predator-prey link has continued unbroken.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi and bacteria that break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the wet soils.

story: Wood Buffalo National Park covers 44,741 square kilometres in northeastern Alberta and the southern Northwest Territories in Canada. Established in 1922, it is the largest national park of Canada. It protects the world's largest herd of free-roaming wood bison and one of two known nesting sites of whooping cranes.
matters: The park preserves the Peace-Athabasca Delta, which is one of the world's largest fresh-water deltas. It is recognized as the most ecologically complete and largest example of the Great Plains-Boreal grassland ecosystem of North America.
